title: Iterative Label Refinement Matters More than Preference Optimization under Weak Supervision

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
Several prior papers address overoptimization in RLHF or alignment under noisy supervision, but none specifically investigate whether the standard SFT+RLHF pipeline remains effective when human supervision is unreliable for hard-to-supervise tasks. Papers [4], [6], [8], and [18] discuss weak-to-strong generalization and unreliable supervision, but they focus on eliciting strong capabilities from weak supervision rather than diagnosing pipeline effectiveness or DPO failure. Papers [1], [2], [3], [12], [13], [14], [16], and [25] study overoptimization in RLHF or DPO, but they do not address the specific purpose of evaluating pipeline robustness under unreliable human supervision. No prior paper establishes the same empirical relationship between unreliable supervision and pipeline effectiveness.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves simulating unreliable supervision using weak LMs (p-tilde and q-tilde) and time-constrained human annotators, then analyzing SFT vs SFT+DPO performance while varying the DPO KL-regularization coefficient beta across feedback-quality levels. Papers [1], [2], [3], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [16], and [25] analyze overoptimization mechanisms in RLHF or DPO, including the role of KL regularization and beta tuning, but none use controlled simulations of unreliable supervision with weak LMs or human annotators. Papers [4], [6], [8], and [18] simulate weak-to-strong setups but do not vary beta or isolate overoptimization mechanisms in the same way. The mechanism is not substantively equivalent to any prior work.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design uses GSM8K, BIRD, and SaferPaca benchmarks with weak-to-strong setups (2B->7B, 7B->70B, 2B->70B), measuring SFT vs SFT+DPO performance under varying feedback quality and beta values. Papers [4], [6], [8], and [18] use weak-to-strong setups and similar benchmarks, and papers [1], [2], [3], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [16], and [25] evaluate overoptimization effects using standard RLHF/DPO benchmarks and metrics. The evaluation design (weak-to-strong setups, beta variation, and performance comparison) is covered by prior work, even though the specific benchmarks and feedback setups differ.

### Domain
The domain is LLM post-training/alignment (RLHF) under unreliable supervision. Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [6], [8], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [16], [18], and [25] all operate in the same general application area of LLM alignment, RLHF, or weak-to-strong generalization under noisy or unreliable supervision. The domain is covered.

### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to provide an alternative to RLHF that better utilizes comparison feedback under unreliable supervision, avoiding DPO's regularization dilemma while still allowing large model updates. Paper [3] discusses RS-DPO, which also aims to address limitations of DPO in the context of LLM alignment, specifically focusing on improving stability and computational efficiency. However, RS-DPO does not explicitly address the issue of unreliable supervision or propose a method to avoid DPO's regularization dilemma while enabling large model updates. Similarly, papers [8], [9], and [11] discuss DPO and its limitations but do not propose a solution to the specific problem of unreliable supervision or the regularization dilemma. Therefore, no prior paper fully covers the purpose of this contribution.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, Iterative Label Refinement (ILR), involves splitting SFT data, training two models to cross-label held-out subsets, using comparison feedback to refine labels, and retraining a fresh SFT model iteratively. Paper [4] introduces Iterative Cross Learning (ICL), which also splits noisy training data into subsets, trains independent models, and uses their predictions to refine labels iteratively. While the specifics differ (e.g., ICL does not use comparison feedback or focus on SFT models), the underlying primitive of iterative cross-labeling and refinement is substantively equivalent. Similarly, papers [1], [5], and [18] describe iterative pseudo-labeling or learning with noisy labels, which also involve iterative refinement of labels, though they do not use comparison feedback or target the same application. Thus, the mechanism is covered by prior work.

### Evaluation
The evaluation involves demonstrating qualitative mechanism insights and quantitative gains, such as larger KL divergence from the initial SFT model compared to DPO and improved SFT-label accuracy over rounds. Papers [3], [8], and [9] evaluate DPO and related methods using similar designs, such as KL divergence comparisons and accuracy improvements over iterations. While the specific benchmarks and datasets differ, the evaluation design (e.g., measuring KL divergence and accuracy improvements) is substantively equivalent. Therefore, the evaluation is covered.

### Domain
The domain is LLM post-training and alignment. Papers [3], [8], [9], and [11] all operate in the same general area of LLM alignment and post-training, even though they may focus on different specific methods or datasets. Thus, the domain is covered.
